## Introduction

Unlike the mid-term, there is no single specification for everyone — so before you list requirements, tell me what you are building. Name the project you chose: one of the ideas on the [Final Project Specifications](../projects/final_project.qmd) page, **or** a project the instructor has approved (say so, and when it was approved).

Then write a few paragraphs (in prose) explaining what you are trying to accomplish. Who is the user? What problem do they have today, and what will they be able to do with your solution that they cannot do now? What is in scope and — just as important — what is out of scope? What does a successful run look like? Finally, make the case for why this problem **needs a multi-agent design** rather than a single prompt or a script.

The project I have chosen is **34.4.13 Sports: Upset Condition Profiler**.

In this project, I aim to forecast potential upsets in NCAA Division I Football Bowl Subdivision utilizing a multi-agent system to research common preconditions of possible upsets in order to determine which current matchups follow those same signals. One user of this project would be an analyst/reporter who covers the sport whose job it is to research, break down, and highlight upcoming matchups. Like with any other sport, football is a high variance game which introduces a substantial amount of noise and luck, which can result in the empirically *better* team losing a specific game, even if they would win \>50% of the time over the span of a thousand simulated games. Typically, 13-14 points is a well-supported estimate for the standard deviation of scoring-margin errors relative to expected margins, which shows that, oftentimes, the best team doesn't always win. The problem today for these analysts is that forecasting potential upsets is tricky, it is something that happens often, but deciding *which* games are the actual upsets is difficult.

Betting markets are also quite accurate, with mainstream sources having an MAE of \~10 points when predicting final scoring margin. So, having to go against the markets can be dangerous. With this tool, analysts can look through advanced metrics and statistics that modelers might use and look at other factors that people and models may overlook like, travel fatigue, revenge games, rest days between games, overlooking opponent for the marquee matchup in their next game, etc. Researching these things isn't impossible for a team of analysts to do, but there are typically dozens of games a day with the addition of all of the other responsibilities the analyst has. With this project, it will streamline the research process by providing the user with its upset predictions and justifications from the list of common factors of past upsets.

It's also important to note what the project can and cannot do or answer. Historical upset research, upcoming matchup monitoring, upset risk scoring, multi-agent orchestration, and explainable recommendations are all features and functionalities that **are** in-scope for this project. On the contrary, guaranteed score predictions and scoring margin, real-time in-game analysis, automated sports betting, functionality outside of NCAA Division I Football Bowl Subdivision, and player-level forecasting are all features that are **not** in-scope. A successful run for this project would be an autonomous system in which the `Upset-Scorer` agent takes the confirmed flags and compiled research from the `Monitor-Orchestrator` to determine which games that day are on upset-watch, ranked 1 to n based on its upset score, along with its explanations. These results would then be presented in the final deliverable of a Streamlit UI.

This project could, in theory, be done in a single-agent system or script, but would have many limitations and ultimately provide unsatisfactory results. Using a single agent, the context would overflow with all of the (mostly irrelevant) information from the different tasks, which would degrade performance. Additionally, we would lose out on all of the parallelizable steps in this project. Also, we would lose the ability to debug and audit as easily.

This project benefits from a multi-agent design due to the specialized tasks required for each of the agents, the want for validation, and the ability to parallelize work during different phases. Additionally, allowing agents to have specialized tasks should keep their context shorter and more focused, along with easier debugging and auditing. A single agent would make these needs more difficult, especially in validation, overload, and not being able to parallelize certain phases of this project.

## Requirements

List the requirements for **your** project, based on the [Final Project Specifications](../projects/final_project.qmd) (the overview, required showcase sections, rubric, and the description of the idea you chose — or your instructor-approved proposal) and on the design you are proposing in your Introduction. List as many as you can (20 is not meaningful here). This is a critical step! Any person or LLM should be able to fully understand **all** requirements for the application from this list.

Number every requirement — the later sections refer back to them by number.

1.  The solution should provide a usable and responsive UI using Python's Streamlit that exposes the solution and shows agent activity.

2.  The solution should let the user sort/filter today's games by certain fields or select certain games for analysis by the `Monitor-Orchestrator` and `Upset-Scorer` agents if they so choose.

3.  The solution should let the user rerun the process as many times as they wish with any combination of games.

4.  The solution should utilize an Orchestrator-worker architecture for the historical ingestion of structured data of the project. Let the `Data-Orchestrator` utilize two workers that retrieve data on past games in batch using ESPN's API.

5.  The solution should let workers for the `Research-Orchestrator` use `Deep Research` and let the `Monitor-Orchestrator` use `Brave` and `Fetch`.

6.  The solution should parallelize the work done by all of the orchestrator agents in order to reduce latency on this long and expensive task.

7.  The solution should let the `Research-Orchestrator` aggregate its findings from its workers. It should also enforce Pydantic's JSON schema and validate JSON results.

8.  The solution should use SQLite to store the corpus, specs, `labeled_games`, and `validated_preconditions`, while ChromaDB is used to hold accepted citations.

9.  The solution should utilize a deterministic labeler and statistical validation tools to take research given by the `Research Worker` agents and data from the `Data-Orchestrator` to determine what common preconditions are actually useful signal in determining potential upsets.

10. The solution should utilize a batch data pipeline that extracts scheduled games for that day using the ESPN API based on what games the user chooses. The API should only return FBS versus FBS matchups, along with team, location, team statistics, weather, and betting odds to determine who is the favorite.

11. The solution should retrieve the daily matchups for the `Monitor-Orchestrator` and Streamlit UI for displaying today's slate of games using the ESPN API.

12. The solution should utilize a `Monitor-Orchestrator` that assigns only the selected games to parallel `Monitor Worker` agents, which use each game's structured data and the `Brave Search` and `Fetch` MCP tools to confirm or drop the flag and attach citations. The workers should return confirmed upset flags with supporting evidence to its orchestrator.

13. The `Monitor-Orchestrator` should provide a rationale for all confirmed flags, explaining why each game is considered a potential upset.

14. The solution should then utilize a `Upset-Scorer` agent, which will take the output from the `Monitor-Orchestrator`, including its rationale and confirmed flags, and use VT ARC's d3-mini decision model with a type of score to rank which upsets are most prone to happen.

15. The solution should let the research pipeline output its final work in a SQLite DB that has tables: `precondition_spec`, `spec_store`, `labeled_games`, and `validated_preconditions`.

16. The solution should provide well-structured code with descriptive comments and run instructions.

17. The solution should let the two `Monitor Workers` run in parallel under the `Monitor-Orchestrator`.

18. The solution should provide the cited rationale and confirmed evidence from the `Monitor-Orchestrator` along with the score from the `Upset-Scorer`'s decision model.

19. The solution should be highly reliable. Running the ranker on the same matchups should generate relatively consistent results. If the results are wildly different, the solution is a complete failure and will never be accepted.

20. The solution should utilize a `.env`, while keeping it separate from Git and using `.env.example` as a boilerplate for the user.

21. The solution should conform to a standardized JSON output using Pydantic to prevent broken handoffs.

22. The solution should properly handle API failures, LLM timeouts, and MCP failures without crashing the whole application.

23. The solution should cache matchups that already have been analyzed.

24. The solution should guarantee that no data known after kickoff can influence a game's label, precondition specification, or upset score by using a deterministic filter `known_at < kickoff_time`.

25. The solution should also validate the upset probabilities produced by the `Upset-Scorer` agent, using seasons 2021-2023 as training data, the 2024 season as the validation set, and 2025 as the testing set. It's important to know that the results being predicted are meaningful.

26. The solution should conduct `Deep Research` once per precondition candidate, not once per game as in the original design. Rules are then applied deterministically across the corpus.

27. The solution should store PreconditionSpecs with a rule, required fields, and thresholds, with versioning, in a SQLite table.

28. The solution should contain a deterministic labeler which is applied to every spec/game and outputs `labeled_games` with evidence trails.

29. The solution should use deterministic screening to evaluate the slate of games. Games that match at least one precondition are then researched further with a web search.

30. The solution should sample a fixed number of labeled games, using `Brave` and `Fetch` to compute precision/recall for testing.

31. The solution should use a False Discovery Rate-corrected approach in its statistical testing using out-of-sample observations.

32. The solution should report non-null percentages for every field, team, and other attribute to identify any missing data.

## LLM / RAG Issues

Referring back to the lectures on LLM and RAG — and, now that you have seen them, on multi-agent systems and anti-patterns — what are the specific issues that you must overcome with good agentic AI design/architecture/patterns **to meet the requirements**? **Make sure you point back to a specific requirement**. Don't solve the issue yet. Just identify it. You should have a fair number of these (between 5 and 20).

1.  For requirement 5, the specific LLM issue that needs to be addressed is hallucinations. Hallucinations can provide confident, but inaccurate responses for a multitude of reasons (e.g., lost-in-the-middle context, context overflow, unclear instructions, etc.). This can especially be a cause for concern for the `Research-Orchestrator` agent who has to read many different documents across different preconditions. If allowed, the evidence used for the `Monitor-Orchestrator` will confidently flag games as an upset using incorrect assumptions about preconditions for upsets.

2.  For requirement 5, the specific LLM issue that needs to be addressed is prompt injection. Prompt injections allow vulnerabilities or faulty information which can influence the LLM into providing incorrect answers. This can be a cause for concern for both the workers under the `Research-Orchestrator` who will read tons of research material from the open web. If allowed, the evidence used for the `Monitor-Orchestrator` will confidently flag games as an upset using incorrect assumptions about preconditions for upsets.

3.  For requirement 9, the specific LLM issue that needs to be addressed is the label noise from vague research output from `Deep Research`. `Deep Research` returns each precondition as prose and is encoded into a `PreconditionSpec`. Then, an underspecified phrase like "short rest" becomes an arbitrary threshold that the `Deterministic Labeler` applies to every game. If allowed, `validated_preconditions` will contain preconditions that are noise rather than signal.

4.  For requirement 19, the specific LLM issue that needs to be addressed is inconsistency and nondeterminism. This issue allows LLMs to output a wide variety of results, essentially making them useless. Ideally, we would like the `Monitor-Orchestrator` and `Upset-Scorer` agents alike to provide mostly consistent results for the same slate of games.

5.  For requirement 21, the specific LLM issue is producing a JSON file following a certain schema. Whenever there is a tool call, or in this case storing structured data into the SQLite database, it's imperative that the JSON output from an LLM follows the required format. Otherwise, the application may crash if the expected JSON schema isn't followed.

6.  For requirement 24, the specific LLM issue that needs to be addressed is data leakage. This mostly comes from data that may have been updated after the game concluded (e.g., weather, closing lines, etc.). On top of that, a `Monitor Worker` fetch can return a page that was published before kickoff, but edited afterwards. If allowed, the `Upset-Scorer` will use information that wasn't known before kickoff, causing the data leakage issue and perhaps inflating testing accuracy.

## Basic Architecture

Write up a couple of paragraphs (in prose) on how you plan to design the solution. What will be the general approach. Don't solve the issues yet... just general approach. What are the major pieces, how do they connect, etc.?

The solution will be architected as a multi-agent system using an orchestrator-worker combined with sequential/pipeline stages. In the first phase, the `Data-Orchestrator` agent will use two workers to parallelize the work by batching `game_id`s to retrieve relevant historical structured data on past games from the ESPN API. These results will then be aggregated by the orchestrator and validated by the Pydantic Validator. After validation, these results will be stored in a SQLite table. This process is a one-time bulk ingestion that will not be user-initiated.

In phase 2, the `Research-Orchestrator` will break up twenty or so different possible preconditions for an upset and partition them across two workers. Each worker will use `Deep Research` for each precondition to collect a definition, operational thresholds, plausible moderators, counter-evidence, and citations. Once returned to the orchestrator, they pass a Pydantic validation check, and the resulting report is written into a SQLite table. Candidates that cannot be encoded as a deterministic rule will be rejected with a provided reason. Then, the `Deterministic Labeler` will look at each spec and apply it to every game in the corpus and save the results in a SQLite table with an evidence trail. The statistical validation tools then estimate effect sizes and CIs, and check out-of-sample predictive validity before promoting into a `validated_preconditions` table. Because it's possible that the labeler step might be wrong, the orchestrator then takes a sample of labels against cited sources using `Brave` and `Fetch` and computes precision and recall. It will then tune the rules where disagreements appear and re-label the corpus with new thresholds. Finally, the accepted citations are embedded with qwen3-embedding:8b and stored in ChromaDB.

In phase 3, the Streamlit UI will request that day's FBS vs. FBS slate using the ESPN API and present it as a sortable, filterable list along with a visually appealing UI using team colors and minimalistic helmet logos. After selecting which games to research (default selected to ALL), the user will click "Analyze" to start. For each run, the `Monitor-Orchestrator` loads the validated preconditions and runs the deterministic rule screen to evaluate every rule against that slate of games. For matchups where at least one validated precondition exists, a web search will commence where the `Monitor Workers` will use `Brave` and `Fetch` to confirm or drop each flag and attach citations. Agent progress is shown in the UI. Confirmed flags will then go to the `Upset-Scorer`, which will use the d3-mini decision model to assign upset probabilities and rank games based on those probabilities with rationale and citations. Analyzed matchups are then cached to reduce latency in the future for repeat runs. Also, we will ensure that every model, tool call, etc. is wrapped to handle timeout failures so the application won't crash or degrade output.

Off to the side, we will also want to validate our results using the upset probability outputs from previous seasons as training data, to determine how this system actually performs. Metrics like log loss and Brier score will be reported along with a calibration plot. Without this, the outputs from the `Upset-Scorer` would be mostly meaningless when the product is first shipped.

You should end your `Basic Architecture` with the level of agency you think is **earned** by this solution architecture. Go back to the beginning of the course for the various levels. **Make sure you give a quick summary of why it is earned.**

The level of agency earned by this solution architecture is a **multi-agent orchestrator-worker design with sequential pipeline stages**. This level of agency is earned because of the need for parallelism in the research workers splitting independent preconditions and the monitor workers splitting work across different games, and because the plan is given upfront. This is different from the Supervisor-Router design that only allows work to be done fully sequentially in an essentially ReAct loop. Also, there is no need for the different workers to communicate with each other, just their respective orchestrator. Compared to a single-agent design, there would simply be too much context in its context window to produce a quality output, especially with unrelated information congesting it.

## Actors

Include: User, Streamlit UI, Data-Orchestrator, Historical-Stats Worker 1, Historical-Stats Worker 2, Research-Orchestrator, Research Worker 1, Research Worker 2, Deep Research (MCP), College Football API, Pydantic Validator, Spec Store, SQLite structured corpus, Deterministic Labeler, Statistical Validation Tools, Brave + Fetch, embedding model (qwen3-embedding:8b), ChromaDB, validated_preconditions table, ESPN API, Monitor-Orchestrator, Deterministic Rule Screen, Monitor Worker 1, Monitor Worker 2, Upset-Scorer agent, d3-mini Decision Model, and Cache.

## Phase 1 — Structured Corpus Ingestion

-   This phase will be a one-off bulk ingestion process, not executed by the user.

-   The `Data-Orchestrator` will have two `Historical-Stats` workers that split the game-ID batches and pull structured data from the ESPN API in parallel. There is no per-game web research in this phase.

-   There will be a loop where the orchestrator partitions pairs of historical game-ID batches across the two `Historical-Stats` workers. Use the loop keyword and the par keyword on the graphic.

-   In the loop, each `Historical-Stats` worker will request the schedule, box scores, team statistics, venue, and rankings from the ESPN API and return the structured game records keyed by `game_id`.

-   After the loop finishes, the orchestrator will aggregate the batches, deduplicate by `game_id`, and send the aggregated JSON to the Pydantic validator.

-   If successful (use the alt keyword), have the orchestrator store the validated JSON in the SQLite structured corpus, confirm storage, and report coverage by season, team, and field.

-   If failed, have the Pydantic validator return the schema and field errors to the orchestrator, have it log the failures and quarantine the invalid records with error details.

-   End the loop and alt.

-   Add a note that only pre-kickoff fields are admitted; closing lines and weather must come from a structured feed captured before kickoff.

## Phase 2 — Precondition Discovery and Validation

-   Like the first diagram, this will be done one time and is not initiated by the user.

-   The `Research-Orchestrator` will have two `Research Workers` that split the candidate preconditions. This phase researches preconditions, not games.

-   There will be a loop where the orchestrator partitions batches of candidate preconditions across the two workers. Use the loop keyword.

-   In a par block (use the par keyword), Research Worker 1 will take its assigned batch and, for each precondition, send a research brief to Deep Research covering the definition, thresholds, moderators, and counter-evidence. Deep Research returns a report, citations, and reported effect sizes, which the worker returns to the orchestrator.

-   In the same par block, Research Worker 2 will do the same for its assigned batch. Use the and keyword between the two workers.

-   End the par and loop.

-   In a second loop, for each returned research report, the orchestrator will send the report to the Pydantic validator to validate the `PreconditionSpec` schema.

-   In an alt block, if the rule can be operationalized, have the validator return a valid spec with the rule, required fields, and thresholds; the orchestrator stores it in the Spec Store and the store confirms.

-   If no encodable rule is returned, have the validator reject it as not operationalizable and the orchestrator log the reason and discard the candidate. End the alt and loop.

-   Have the orchestrator retrieve all operationalizable specs from the Spec Store.

-   Have the orchestrator send the specs to the Deterministic Labeler. The labeler reads historical games from the SQLite structured corpus, including schedule, rankings, venues, weather, and closing lines, and evaluates each rule for each game. It returns `labeled_games` with evidence trails to the orchestrator.

-   Have the orchestrator submit the labels to the statistical validation tools, which estimate effect sizes and confidence intervals, test statistical significance with FDR correction, evaluate out-of-sample predictive validity, and return the results and diagnostics.

-   In an alt block, if the preconditions pass the acceptance criteria, have the orchestrator store them with thresholds and citations in the `validated_preconditions` table and confirm storage. If they fail, have the orchestrator reject and log the reason.

-   Have the orchestrator spot-check labels on sampled games using Brave + Fetch, which return cited articles. The orchestrator computes labeler precision and recall and tunes the rules.

-   In an opt block (use the opt keyword), if the rules changed during the spot-check, have the orchestrator re-label the corpus, get updated `labeled_games`, re-test the updated labels, get updated statistics, and update the stored thresholds and statistics in `validated_preconditions`.

-   Finally, have the orchestrator embed the accepted citations with qwen3-embedding:8b, receive the vectors, store the chunks and metadata in ChromaDB, and confirm ingestion.

## Phase 3 — Daily Matchup Monitoring + Upset Ranking

-   The user will open the Condition Profiler app via the Streamlit UI.

-   The UI will request today's FBS vs. FBS slate from the ESPN API, which returns the schedule, teams, records, and betting odds, and display the matchups as sortable and filterable.

-   In a large loop, the user will be able to select any combination of games, or all of them by default, and click Analyze.

-   After the user clicks Analyze, the UI will initialize an agent progress tracker and submit the selected game IDs to the Monitor-Orchestrator.

-   The Monitor-Orchestrator will load the validated preconditions from the `validated_preconditions` table, which returns the rules, thresholds, and citations.

-   The Monitor-Orchestrator will send every selected game to the Deterministic Rule Screen first, which evaluates all rules on structured fields and returns a shortlist of games tripping one or more rules. This happens before any web research.

-   In an alt block, if the shortlist is empty, have the orchestrator return that there are no upset alerts for the slate.

-   If the shortlist has candidates, have the orchestrator partition the shortlist across two Monitor Workers.

-   In a par block (use the par keyword), Monitor Worker 1 will take its assigned games and matched rules. For each game, it will Brave search for week-specific context, fetch the cited pages, confirm or drop the flag, attach citations, report per-game progress to the orchestrator, and have the orchestrator update the UI. It then returns confirmed flags with evidence to the orchestrator.

-   In the same par block, Monitor Worker 2 will do the same for its assigned games. Use the and keyword between the workers.

-   End the par block. Have the orchestrator aggregate and deduplicate the worker results.

-   In an alt block, if one or more games are confirmed, have the orchestrator send the confirmed flags and evidence to the Upset-Scorer. The scorer will use the d3-mini decision model to estimate upset probabilities, rank the games by predicted upset risk, and return the rankings, probabilities, and evidence to the orchestrator, which sends the ranked alerts to the UI. If all candidates were dropped, have the orchestrator return that there are no qualifying upset alerts.

-   After the analysis, have the UI cache the analyzed matchups and results, confirm the cache write, mark the analysis complete, and display the rankings, reasoning, and citations to the user.

-   End the loop and alt blocks.

```{mermaid}
    RO->>RO: Compute labeler precision and recall, tune rules

    opt Rules changed during spot-check
        RO->>LB: Re-label corpus with tuned rules
        LB-->>RO: Updated labeled_games
        RO->>ST: Re-test updated labels
        ST-->>RO: Updated statistics
        RO->>VP: Update stored thresholds and statistics
        VP-->>RO: Confirm update
    end

    RO->>EMB: Embed accepted citations
    EMB-->>RO: Embedding vectors
    RO->>VDB: Store chunks and metadata
    VDB-->>RO: Confirm ingestion complete
```

## Phase 3 Diagram — Daily Matchup Monitoring + Upset Ranking

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6.5
%%| fig-height: 8
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {'sequence': {'diagramMarginY': 80}}}%%

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor U as User
    participant UI as Streamlit UI
    participant ESPN as ESPN API
    participant MO as Monitor-Orchestrator
    participant DB as SQLite (validated_preconditions)
    participant SCR as Deterministic Rule Screen
    participant W1 as Monitor Worker 1
    participant W2 as Monitor Worker 2
    participant BF as Brave + Fetch
    participant SC as Upset-Scorer
    participant D3 as d3-mini Decision Model
    participant CA as Cache

    Note over MO,SCR: Deterministic rules screen the full slate before any web research

    U->>UI: Open Condition Profiler
    UI->>ESPN: Request today's FBS vs. FBS slate
    ESPN-->>UI: Schedule, teams, records, and betting odds
    UI-->>U: Display sortable and filterable matchups

    loop Each user-initiated analysis run
        U->>UI: Select games (all by default) and click Analyze
        UI->>UI: Initialize agent progress tracker
        UI->>MO: Submit selected game IDs

        MO->>DB: Load validated preconditions
        DB-->>MO: Rules, thresholds, and citations

        MO->>SCR: Screen every selected game
        SCR->>SCR: Evaluate all rules on structured fields
        SCR-->>MO: Shortlist of games tripping one or more rules
        MO-->>UI: Report screening complete

        alt Shortlist is empty
            MO-->>UI: No upset alerts for this slate
        else Shortlist has candidates
            MO->>MO: Partition shortlist across workers

            par Monitor Worker 1
                MO->>W1: Assign games and matched rules
                loop Each assigned game
                    W1->>BF: Brave search for week-specific context
                    BF-->>W1: Search results and snippets
                    W1->>BF: Fetch cited pages
                    BF-->>W1: Page content
                    W1->>W1: Confirm or drop flag, attach citations
                    W1-->>MO: Per-game progress
                    MO-->>UI: Update Worker 1 progress
                end
                W1-->>MO: Confirmed flags with evidence
            and Monitor Worker 2
                MO->>W2: Assign games and matched rules
                loop Each assigned game
                    W2->>BF: Brave search for week-specific context
                    BF-->>W2: Search results and snippets
                    W2->>BF: Fetch cited pages
                    BF-->>W2: Page content
                    W2->>W2: Confirm or drop flag, attach citations
                    W2-->>MO: Per-game progress
                    MO-->>UI: Update Worker 2 progress
                end
                W2-->>MO: Confirmed flags with evidence
            end

            MO->>MO: Aggregate and deduplicate worker results

            alt One or more games confirmed
                MO->>SC: Send confirmed flags and evidence
                SC->>D3: Evaluate matchup context and signals
                D3-->>SC: Estimated upset probabilities
                SC->>SC: Rank games by predicted upset risk
                SC-->>MO: Rankings, probabilities, and evidence
                MO-->>UI: Send ranked upset alerts
            else All candidates dropped on confirmation
                MO-->>UI: Return no qualifying upset alerts
            end
        end

        UI->>CA: Cache analyzed matchups and results
        CA-->>UI: Confirm cache write
        UI->>UI: Mark analysis complete
        UI-->>U: Display rankings, reasoning, and citations
    end
```

## Solution Mitigations

Now for each of the LLM/RAG issues, you should give specific design patterns that we learned in class to address them. I need a short explanation of why your solution is the right one. **Make sure you refer back to the numbered issue from the previous section.**

1.  For issue 1, the design pattern that addresses this issue is limiting the amount of information the worker agents can use at a time. In my design, the Orchestrator will send out batches of preconditions at a time for the workers to work on. In doing so, this can limit the amount of content and allow more focused content in their context-window to mitigate hallucinations. Also, we need to account for lost-in-the-middle context by putting more relevant content in the front or back to produce better results for the agents. These are the best approaches because letting the workers in the research phase collect documents from different preconditions would lead to a polluted context window and hallucinations.

2.  For issue 2, the design pattern that addresses this issue is manually whitelisting a set of websites the worker agents can use to extract information. Essentially, only gather data from reliable websites like ESPN.com, Sports-Reference.com, etc., along with local media to prevent any direct or indirect prompt injections that may throw off the final outputs. The reason why this is the best approach is because it's the simplest but most effective way to ensure the content feeding into my workers is legitimate and with no malicious intent as opposed to just telling the LLM "Make sure the website is legitimate".

3.  For issue 3, the design pattern that addresses this issue is a schema gate that only accepts an operational rule with a field, an operator, a threshold, and units, before anything gets entered into the spec store. If `Deep Research` comes back with prose that cannot be written that way, the candidate is rejected with the reason logged. The reason why I think this is the best choice is because it turns an ambiguous definition into something the labeler can apply the same way every time.

4.  For issue 4, the design pattern that addresses this issue is using the d3-mini decision model to take the outputs from the `Monitor-Orchestrator` and its explanations and let the `Upset-Scorer` agent use that model to score the most likely upsets. Decision models like d3-mini have been shown to provide more consistent answers because they score candidates based on a probability distribution as opposed to sampling output tokens. That is why I think it's the best choice instead of using a traditional LLM, which would more likely be less consistent and add latency.

5.  For issue 5, the design pattern that addresses this issue is implementing a validation check for the output JSON structure. Using Pydantic is a good start, but even then, the output may still contain invalid JSON syntax, incorrect data types, invalid values, etc. So, we should use the Orchestrator to help validate the responses from its workers. The reason why I think this is the best choice is because we are already using the Orchestrator as the centralized coordination amongst its workers, making it an obvious choice for it to validate the JSON responses.

6.  For issue 6, the design pattern that addresses this issue is a deterministic timestamp on every field instead of letting the agent decide what should count before kickoff. Every structured column should have a `known_at` time, every fetch should carry a `report_time`, and anything missing or dated after kickoff is discarded before the `Upset-Scorer` sees it. The reason why I think this is the best approach is because it's a simple, deterministic way to achieve no data leakage every time, instead of leaving it in the hands of an LLM to guess it.

## Final Thoughts

Just like the mid-term, this exercise is something you do before invoking an agentic harness. This is where you add value and earn your place in the future AI ecosystem. Next steps we will review this architecture with a frontier level model and refine it. Then we work with an agentic harness to build it!

For this project-planning phase, I had to delve deeper into the many different types of multi-agent designs in order to determine which approach worked best for my project. Having to weigh the pros and cons of each helped me learn more about each of the different centralized and decentralized approaches. Additionally, it made me expand on the feedback from the midterm project for the possible LLM/RAG issues along with its mitigations. Also, this assignment forced me to think about and research the best ways to mitigate hallucinations, context rot, latency, etc. in multi-agent designs that were not present in the midterm project.
